title: VTV Asks You to Pay Yesterday's Premium for Tomorrow's Growth
detail:
VTV Asks You to Pay Yesterday's Premium for Tomorrow's Growth
Trefis Team
Thu, July 30, 2026 at 6:39 AM PDT 4 min read
VVIAX
IWM
SPY
USFD
DIA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

The fund is asking a higher price than usual, but the brisk earnings of its biggest companies might just back it up.

The five largest holdings in the Vanguard Value ETF (VTV) make up 15.0% of the fund, well above what you'd expect if all 331 positions were equally weighted, a reminder that even a broad index leans more heavily on its largest names than its size alone would suggest. When you buy a share of VTV, you're buying a piece of every company in the CRSP US Large Cap Value Index. The real question for an investor today is a simple one: is the price you're paying for that basket of stocks justified by what's actually inside?

A Price Tag Above the Average

Let's start with the price tag. VTV currently trades at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 22.7. To put that number in context, you have to compare it to the fund's own history. Over the last five years, its P/E has averaged 19.4, with a low of 17.8. Today's multiple of 22.7 is about 17% above that five-year average. On this backward-looking measure, you are paying a clear premium compared to recent history.

Is Strong Growth Earning the Premium?

The case for paying that premium rests on the earnings power of the companies VTV holds. And here, the story gets more interesting. The fund's largest holdings, which include companies like Micron Technology at 4.9% of the fund and JPMorgan Chase at 3.1%, saw their earnings per share grow about 25% over the past year. Looking forward, consensus estimates project one-year earnings growth for the fund's holdings at about 17%.

Alongside that growth outlook, the fund's forward price-to-earnings ratio sits at about 15.7x, notably lower than the trailing 22.7x. That gap is wider than the 17% growth estimate alone would explain, because the two multiples aren't measuring the same thing: the forward figure is a non-GAAP number calculated only on profitable holdings, while the trailing 22.7 is a GAAP figure across all holdings. The gap reflects that difference in basis as much as it reflects growth expectations, so it shouldn't be read as the market pricing in 45% earnings growth.

The Vanishing Cushion

But there's a significant counterpoint to consider: opportunity cost. On a trailing basis, the aggregate earnings yield of the fund's holdings is 4.4%. At the same time, a 10-year US Treasury, the benchmark for a risk-free investment, yields 4.7%. This means that, using today's earnings, the fund offers a negative risk premium. It means you are accepting the inherent risks of owning stocks for a potential return currently lower than what you could get from government bonds. On a forward basis, using the same profitable-holdings estimate behind the 15.7 forward P/E, the earnings yield would be closer to 6.4%, above the Treasury yield. The cushion, then, isn't absent so much as conditional: it depends entirely on whether that projected 17% earnings growth actually comes through.

title: SPMO ETF Hides A Heavy Tech Tilt

SPMO ETF Hides A Heavy Tech Tilt

Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

A fund's label tells you the strategy, but rarely reveals the concentrated bets you are actually making.

More than half of the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF (SPMO) is invested in a single sector: Information Technology accounts for 54% of the fund. The fund is designed to track an index of S&P 500 stocks showing strong recent performance. But looking under the hood reveals that this momentum is not evenly spread across the market.

How Concentrated Is The Portfolio?

The fund's ten largest holdings make up 52% of its total assets. And while it holds 101 positions, its portfolio behaves like a much smaller collection of about 26 equally weighted holdings. The concentration is clear at the very top, where a single company, Micron Technology, represents 10.8% of the fund. It is joined in the top five by names like Nvidia and Broadcom, cementing the fund's specific character.

What Is The Real Industry Exposure?

That character is overwhelmingly technological. The Information Technology sector's 54% share is more than four times larger than the next biggest sector, Industrials, at 12.8%. Within tech, the focus sharpens considerably. The Semiconductors industry alone accounts for 34% of the entire fund. When combined with Semiconductor Materials & Equipment at 7.7%, the bet on chip-related stocks becomes even clearer. Even the largest technology mega-caps, often called the Magnificent 7, make up a distinct 16.3% slice of the fund.

Is This The Bet You Intended To Make?

The name 'S&P 500 Momentum' suggests a broad strategy. The reality is a portfolio with a heavy lean into a specific corner of the market: technology, and semiconductors in particular. Knowing a fund's true composition is especially important after a period of strong returns. For investors thinking about how to manage gains in their portfolio, it can be helpful to consider different strategies. This concentration is not a flaw; it is simply the outcome of the fund's rules-based approach to finding momentum. The key question for an investor is whether this focused exposure aligns with their goals, or if it unintentionally doubles down on a tech position they already hold elsewhere.

Is This A Fair-Value Way To Own It?

Seeing what is inside SPMO is half the picture. The other half is whether you are getting that exposure at a fair price and a competitive return, or whether a similar fund delivers much the same holdings for less.

Our ETF Valuation and Performance Scorecard ranks the major funds side by side on valuation versus their own history, trailing and risk-adjusted return, volatility and expense ratio, so you can see whether SPMO is a sensible way to own what it holds, and which comparable funds give you a similar basket on better terms.

detail:
AI's Biggest Winners Are Selling Off, and ETFs Are Behaving Strangely
Sumit Roy

Bear Market

The biggest winners of the AI trade have turned volatile, and that volatility is creating some unusual dynamics across the ETF landscape. After an extraordinary run in the second quarter, semiconductor stocks have been hit hard in the third as investors take profits and start to worry about when the cycle finally peaks.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) has fallen 27% since it hit an all-time high on June 22. The damage hasn't stayed contained to chips, either. Some of the Magnificent Seven stalwarts have struggled alongside them, with Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon all under pressure.

That combination has dragged the tech-heavy Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) sharply lower, and it's now down about 10% from its highs. The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) has fared even worse, off more than 14%.

On the other hand, the broader market, and especially stocks that sit outside of tech, have held up far better, and in some cases have kept climbing. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) is down just 3% from its high, even with the double-digit declines in QQQ and XLK.

Tech carries the heaviest weighting in the S&P 500, but other sectors have absorbed the blow. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP), which weights every S&P 500 stock equally and blunts the influence of tech, illustrates this well. It hit an all-time high on Tuesday, the same session that semiconductor stocks got pounded and QQQ dropped close to 1%.

Still, despite the volatility in tech, this looks like an ordinary pullback so far, even if a violent one. On a year-to-date basis the AI and semiconductor trade is still doing extremely well. 

SOXX is up 58%, XLK is up 18%, and QQQ is up 10%. All three are beating VOO, which sits closer to 9%. RSP is the standout. Its 14% gain is beating both VOO and QQQ.





That said, while RSP is doing well in 2026, equal weighting the S&P 500 has underperformed for years. The biggest of the big kept getting bigger, and any strategy that trimmed them fell behind. 

This year that has flipped. With most of the Mag 7 lagging, tilting smaller has actually helped. Semiconductors have been phenomenal year to date, but the megacap giants like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Tesla have not kept pace.

The one standout among the giants has been Apple, which hit an all-time high this week. It's a little bit ironic, since it's the only one of the group not spending aggressively on the AI capex boom.

title: The SOXX Dip Has A Painful History
detail:
The SOXX Dip Has A Painful History
Trefis Team
Wed, July 29, 2026 at 3:05 PM PDT 4 min read
SOXX
IWM
NVDA
QQQ
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

Before you add to your position, understand what the fund's own past says about the extra downside that often comes first.

For anyone buying a dip in the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), history suggests the first move was often another lurch down. The median worst further drawdown in the year after a dip was 20%, a steep price to pay when you're already looking at a fund that is down about 25% from its 52-week high. That figure is the key to understanding whether a discount like this one has historically been a bargain or just the start of more pain.

Did The Rebound Justify The Ride?

The historical record is two-sided. Since 2005, SOXX has fallen 20% or more on 6 separate occasions. Of those 6 dips, 4 were followed by a positive return over the next twelve months. When the fund did recover, the gains were significant. The median return in the twelve months after a dip was +28%.

Looking at specific episodes gives a clearer picture. The dip in June 2022 was followed by a 43% gain a year later. The one in February 2016 saw the fund rise 73% over the next twelve months. These are the kinds of outcomes that make dip-buying so tempting. But it's crucial to remember that these gains often came only after a buyer endured that typical 20% further drop first.

A Concentrated Basket, Not A Broad Bet

The reason for the sharp swings, both down and up, lies in what SOXX actually holds. This isn't a sprawling, diversified market index. It's a concentrated fund with just 30 positions, focused entirely on one of the market's most volatile industries. Its five largest holdings make up 38% of the fund, and the top ten account for 61%.

You're making a focused play on the biggest names in semiconductors, with heavyweights like Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Micron Technology (MU), and Nvidia (NVDA) at the top. When this narrow group does well, the fund can deliver returns like the +104% it posted over the past year. But when the sector turns, the concentration works in reverse, and the floor can be a long way down. This kind of volatility is common in semiconductor funds, and a look at a peer fund can offer more perspective on the sector's behavior.

The fund's own history gives a split verdict. The record shows that rebounds have been frequent and often strong. But it also shows that buying a dip has historically meant stomaching another 20% drop first. The answer depends on whether you see that potential for more downside as a price worth paying for a concentrated stake in the semiconductor industry. A broad, diversified fund tends to find its footing more easily. For a focused basket like this one, recovery hinges on the fortunes of just 30 companies.

How Much Eli Lilly (LLY) Are You Really Betting On?

Without you picking it, a single pharmaceutical stock may have quietly become one of the largest positions inside your funds.

Pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly (LLY) is held across 50 equity funds we track, and in some cases, it has grown into a truly significant position. If you own broad health care ETFs, you likely have more exposure to this one company than you think. The stock's performance has been remarkable, but that same run-up has created a concentrated risk that you never actively chose to take on.

How Stretched Has The Stock Become?

Eli Lilly (LLY) has delivered a powerful return of +51% over the past year, with much of that coming in the last three months, which saw a +41% gain. That performance has left the stock trading at $ 1,220.66 (as of July 28, 2026), about 20% above its 200-day moving average. While investors are clearly optimistic, with the stock priced at about 35 times its expected earnings for the year ahead, that gap above its own long-term trend is a simple measure of how far and fast it has moved.

Which Funds Carry The Heaviest Load?

The funds most exposed to Eli Lilly's run are also the ones carrying the most single-stock risk going forward. The State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLV), for example, holds LLY at about 16.1% of the fund and returned +24% over the past year. The Vanguard Health Care ETF (VHT) has about 14.2% of its assets in LLY and returned +27% over the same period. This serves as a reminder that LLY's weight in a fund doesn't map cleanly onto that fund's total return, since dozens of other holdings are moving too. This kind of weighting raises natural questions about portfolio diversification.

What A Simple Pullback Would Cost

This is not a prediction, but a scenario to make the risk concrete. If LLY simply fell back to its 200-day average, it would represent a drop of about 17% from its current price. For the funds holding it, the math is direct. In that scenario, XLV would lose about 2.7% from this one holding alone. VHT would lose about 2.4% from its LLY position. Even a more diversified fund like the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG), with a 4.2% weight, would see a 0.7% drag from this single name.

The problem is that this exposure is sticky. You can't surgically sell just the LLY shares inside your ETF. To reduce your position, you have to sell the entire fund, which could trigger a taxable capital gain on years of appreciation. This tax trap often leads investors to let the concentration quietly build.

What I have discovered throughout my investing career is that stocks and markets tend to top when news seems most bullish and bottom when the news seems the most bearish. Below are two examples from 2026:

Micron Tops on Blowout Earnings Report

In late June, AI leader Micron (MU) reported earnings that blew past Wall Street estimates. In fact, Micron management said that it expects to generate more EPS in 2026 than it has in the past decade. Revenue grew an eye-popping 346% YoY to a record $41.46 billion. Additionally, the company secured 16 strategic agreements worth a minimum of $100 billion. 

Zacks Investment Research


Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Although MU shares initially jumped, the blowout report marked the for the stock and it is down 34% since.

Zacks Investment Research


Image Source: TradingView

Equities Bottom Despite U.S Iran War

An example of a bottom on poor news was the market in late March. At the time, President Trump was threatening to target Iran's oil hubs, generators, and key infrastructure. After weeks of falling, the Nasdaq 100 QQQ began to rise despite bad news and further escalations. It wasn't until April 8th that investors would fully understand what the bullish, resilient price action was discounting – a ceasefire announcement between the U.S. and Iran.

Zacks Investment Research


Image Source: TradingView

Price Action Versus News Takeaway

Tracking the news or fundamentals in a vacuum is futile. Instead, investors should monitor the price action relative to news. For instance, investors should lean bullish if stocks are resilient in the face of bad news and vice versa. Currently, stocks are falling amid AI and renewed geopolitical concerns. If bad news continues to hit the tape and stocks begin to rally anyway, it may be an early signal to investors that the market is ready to bottom.

A fund's label tells you the category, but a look at the holdings ledger reveals the actual shape of your investment.

While the Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (SOXQ) holds 32 different stocks, the fund's portfolio behaves like about 18 equally weighted holdings. That small gap between the number on the box and the reality of the portfolio is where the real story of any index fund lives. The fund aims to track the performance of the largest U.S.-listed companies in the semiconductor business, giving investors exposure to the building blocks of modern electronics.

But an exchange-traded fund is more than just a list of names. It is a basket where some holdings carry far more weight than others. Understanding that weighting is key to knowing what you truly own.

How Many Bets Are You Really Making?

The fund's concentration becomes clear when you look at the top of the portfolio. The ten largest holdings make up 62% of the fund's total assets. This means the performance of a handful of companies has an outsized impact on the fund's daily moves. The single largest holding is Nvidia (NVDA) at 12.4% of the fund, followed by other industry heavyweights like Broadcom (AVGO) and Micron Technology (MU).

When just a few names command this much of the portfolio, their fortunes disproportionately shape your returns. This kind of focused exposure is common in thematic funds, and a look inside another popular semiconductor ETF reveals a similar structure.

Where Is The Money Actually Going?

The fund's name promises semiconductor exposure, and it delivers. But even within that category, the capital is tilted toward specific corners of the industry. The fund is almost entirely in the Information Technology sector, but the breakdown inside is what matters. The Semiconductors sub-industry accounts for 75% of the fund. The next-largest slice is Semiconductor Materials & Equipment, which makes up 23% of the portfolio.

Together, these two slivers of the market define nearly the entire fund. The result is an investment heavily weighted toward chip designers and the companies that supply them with manufacturing machinery.

Is This The Shape You Intended?

Knowing a fund's internal composition is not about judging it as good or bad. It is about alignment. The Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF offers a distinct, concentrated position on the semiconductor industry. The key question for an investor is whether this specific shape, with its heavy reliance on a few top names and sub-industries, is the exposure you were looking for, or if it doubles up on bets you have already made elsewhere in your portfolio.

The healthcare fund just printed a record high, but cashing out of a steady compounder is often the wrong move.

A new high always feels like a moment of decision. For holders of the State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLV), that moment is now. The fund just closed at $167.26, its highest level ever, after a +16.6% run over the past three months. When you see a gain like that, the natural question is whether to hold on, trim your stake, or get out entirely. XLV is an exchange-traded fund designed to give you a slice of the healthcare industry within the S&P 500, holding everything from pharmaceuticals to medical equipment companies.

How Solid Is This New Peak?

Before you act, it is worth looking at what drove this high. First, this is a concentrated fund. Its holdings sit "almost entirely in one sector, Health Care," making it a single-industry allocation. The recent advance was also driven by a few key names. While participation was wide, with 24 of the 30 largest holdings rising over the past three months, the actual heavy lifting was done by a few. The "three biggest movers accounted for about 56% of the up-and-down price movement" among those top 30 holdings. On top of that, the basket is not cheap by its own historical standards. The fund's holdings now trade at about 31.0 times earnings, compared to a roughly 5-year median of 26.8 for this fund.

So, What Should A Holder Do Now?

With the fund looking stretched and trading at a richer valuation, the temptation to sell is real. But for a long-term investor, the most sensible action is often the hardest one: do nothing. A new high, by itself, is not a signal to sell a quality asset. It is what you want your investments to do. This is compounding at work. Selling a fund that holds 63 positions across a vital sector just because it's performing well can be a classic mistake, forcing you to pay taxes and find a new home for your capital. The price of earning long-term returns includes weathering volatility. The fund's deepest fall in recent years was 17.1%, a figure that provides context for what a significant pullback could look like.

The fund currently sits about 10.3% above its 200-day moving average, which confirms it has run ahead of its trend. The only strong reason to act may have nothing to do with the market and everything to do with your own plan. If this strong performance has made your XLV position significantly larger than its target weight in your portfolio, trimming it back into line is simply disciplined rebalancing. This question of what to do at a new high is not unique to healthcare; other sectors like financials are facing similar moments.
